articleMarkdown:
# Learning from The Gentle (Xùn): advance gently while keeping clear judgment

A gentle approach can help things progress gradually, but yielding should not cost you direction, boundaries, or the ability to decide.

Wind can enter small spaces and steadily affect its surroundings without always appearing as a violent impact. Xun is often associated with yielding, entering, and gradual influence, yet its lines also describe repeated hesitation, excessive lowering of oneself, and the loss of resources and an axe. Gentleness needs to be considered alongside clear, proportionate action.

巽 is hexagram 57 in the traditional King Wen sequence, with the symbol ䷸. Its lower trigram is 巽☴ and its upper trigram is 巽☴, traditionally associated with wind and wind respectively. Count the lines from the bottom: 初六, 九二, 九三, 六四, 九五, 上九. A solid line is yang; a broken line is yin. Nine and six identify yang and yin in the line labels; they do not add extra lines.

Line structure (bottom to top): 0 1 1 0 1 1

Six-line figure, displayed top to bottom; line numbering starts at the bottom.

```text
━━━━━━━━━  上九
━━━━━━━━━  九五
━━━━ ━━━━  六四
━━━━━━━━━  九三
━━━━━━━━━  九二
━━━━ ━━━━  初六
```

## The judgment

巽：小亨。利有攸往。利見大人。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Gentle penetration: limited favorable progress. Having somewhere to go is beneficial. Meeting a great person is beneficial.

Legge explains Xun through flexibility and penetration, connecting it with gradual correction and carrying out instructions. “Limited favorable progress” does not mean that gentle people can accomplish only small things; rather, the hexagram’s wording retains a sense of degree and conditions.

For modern study, begin with listening, explanation, and sustained small adjustments, and ask experienced people to help clarify the problem. Meeting a great person does not require dependence on authority. Nor can “yielding” cancel the right to object or refuse unreasonable demands.

Sources: [zhouyi-57](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/巽&oldid=10644966), [legge1882-57](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## Interpretation in the Ten Wings

The Commentary on the Judgment and the Commentary on the Images belong to the Yi Zhuan, the commentaries usually called the “Ten Wings.” Here their explanations are kept distinct from the judgment and line texts, before turning to modern applications for study.

The Commentary on the Judgment says that repeated Xun renews commands. The Commentary on the Images takes successive winds as its image and speaks of reiterating instructions and carrying out affairs. Its concern is not only a gentle manner, but whether meaning is conveyed and work actually done.

Applied here to ordinary cooperation, important explanations need clarity, suitable repetition, and confirmation that the other person understands. Clear explanation is neither repeated nagging nor vague hints. Letting someone know what to do is more effective than merely expecting them to read expressions and tone.

Sources: [zhouyi-57](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/巽&oldid=10644966), [hon-sep](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/chinese-change/)

## 初六 · Hesitation calls for a clear basis for action

進退，利武人之貞。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Advancing and retreating. The constancy of a warrior is beneficial.

Repeated advancing and retreating is followed by the warrior’s constancy, contrasting yielding with decisiveness. Legge understands a need for vigorous, firm judgment, not a demand to use force.

If you keep changing a small decision, first write down the criteria and missing information. Verify what needs verification, then act when there is sufficient basis. You need not wait for everyone to express precisely the same opinion.

Sources: [zhouyi-57](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/巽&oldid=10644966), [legge1882-57](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 九二 · Distinguish ancient inquiry from modern verification

巽在牀下，用史巫紛若，吉无咎。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Yielding beneath the bed, employing scribes and shamans in abundance. Favorable, without blame.

The space beneath a bed and numerous scribes and shamans preserve an ancient scene of divination and religious activity. Legge interprets this as searching for something hidden with the help of scribes and shamans. That is his route of commentary.

A modern analogy is carefully looking for unobvious problems and asking appropriate people to verify them. Ancient shamans provide no basis for real-world exorcism or supernatural diagnosis. Questions still need support from verifiable information.

Sources: [zhouyi-57](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/巽&oldid=10644966), [legge1882-57](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 九三 · Repeated effort is not necessarily genuine depth

頻巽，吝。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Repeated yielding; embarrassment.

Legge reads repeated Xun as impatient, repeated attempts to penetrate, with considerable effort but disproportionate results.

Continually editing an email while never stating the central request may only increase anxiety. Pause to establish what you mean to communicate, rather than mistaking additional repetition for a resolved communication problem.

Sources: [zhouyi-57](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/巽&oldid=10644966), [legge1882-57](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 六四 · Action should produce results people can use

悔亡，田獲三品。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Regret disappears. The hunt brings game for three uses.

The hunt yields three kinds of game. Legge explains these through uses such as sacrifice, hospitality, and cooking. The line does not mean that a reader will obtain three payments or three rewards.

In ordinary cooperation, check whether effort produces clear, useful results: a problem explained, responsibility confirmed, or a next step someone can take. Results need to fit the purpose, not merely look more numerous.

Sources: [zhouyi-57](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/巽&oldid=10644966), [legge1882-57](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 九五 · Attend carefully to both sides of a change

貞吉悔亡，无不利。无初有終，先庚三日，後庚三日，吉。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Constancy is favorable; regret disappears, and nothing is disadvantageous. No good beginning, but an ending. Three days before geng and three days after geng: favorable.

Legge interprets the days before and after geng as giving notice before a change and checking afterward. The ancient date structure draws attention to both sides; it should not be mechanically converted into a universal six-day implementation plan.

When adjusting a routine rule, explain the reason and impact first, then observe problems arising in use. An imperfect beginning can still be corrected, but “having an ending” requires concrete follow-through.

Sources: [zhouyi-57](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/巽&oldid=10644966), [legge1882-57](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## 上九 · Excessive yielding can erode the ability to act

巽在牀下，喪其資斧，貞凶。

Original editorial rendering, not a quotation from Legge: Yielding beneath the bed, losing resources and the axe. Even with right constancy, the outcome is unfavorable.

The image beneath the bed returns, but now resources and an axe are lost, and the outcome becomes unfavorable. Legge uses the lost axe of decision to explain the danger of excessive yielding and states that he follows a textual adjustment from an older commentary.

Check whether fear of displeasing others prevents you from ever stating real limits. Respect for others and your own judgment can coexist. A lack of boundaries should not be called the best possible cooperative attitude.

Sources: [zhouyi-57](https://zh.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=周易/巽&oldid=10644966), [legge1882-57](https://tianmu.org/good-work-library/confucian/general-texts/the-i-ching-james-legge)

## Making a new working agreement genuinely clear

Original modern scenario

A group wants every submitted item to identify its sources consistently. The coordinator first explains which repeated inquiries this will reduce and gives a simple example, inviting members to point out inconvenient parts of the existing process.

Once the practice begins, she examines why entries are missing and discovers that some people do not know how to record oral sources. She adds guidance. For information clearly required, she maintains the standard rather than abandoning it to preserve harmony.

The change gradually takes hold through clear explanation, feedback, and appropriate firmness. Learning from Xun is not about influencing others covertly; it is about gently making meaning clear and putting it into practice.

## Avoiding misreadings

- Xun does not endorse manipulation, people-pleasing, or unlimited obedience, and does not make the scene of scribes and shamans a basis for supernatural diagnosis.

- The days before and after geng are not a personal lucky-date algorithm. Whether yielding is appropriate depends on actual boundaries and consequences.

## Three exercises

1. Rewrite a vague request as one sentence another person can understand and act on.

2. Determine whether the other person is unwilling, does not understand, or cannot act under the actual conditions.

3. Write down one boundary you need to express clearly so that gentleness does not become unconditional agreement.

## Related reading

Dui — Joy (hexagram-58): Xun emphasizes gentle communication and implementation; Dui emphasizes joy and sincerity in exchange. Neither can be reduced to making people comfortable: both need real substance and appropriate proportion.

When reading Xun, ask: has my gentleness made matters clearer, or kept the words that really need saying unspoken?
